symptoms: Elevated blood glucose (hyperglycemia), hypoglycemia (from treatment), visual impairment, injection site reactions, lipodystrophy
indications: For the treatment of diabetes mellitus in adults, adolescents and children aged 2 years and above.
mechanism_of_action: Insulin glargine is a recombinant human insulin analogue (21A-Gly-30Ba-L-Arg-30Bb-L-Arg-human insulin) designed to have a low solubility at neutral pH. At pH 4 (as in the Lantus injection solution) it is completely soluble. After injection into the subcutaneous tissue the acidic solution is neutralised leading to formation of micro-precipitates from which small amounts of insulin glargine are continuously released providing a smooth, peakless, predictable concentration/time profile with a prolonged duration of action. The primary activity of insulin including insulin glargine is regulation of glucose metabolism. Insulin and its analogues lower blood glucose levels by stimulating peripheral glucose uptake especially by skeletal muscle and fat and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Insulin inhibits lipolysis in the adipocyte, inhibits proteolysis and enhances protein synthesis. Insulin glargine is metabolised into 2 active metabolites M1 (21A-Gly-insulin) and M2 (21A-Gly-des-30B-Thr-insulin).
composition: Lantus® SoloStar® 100IU/mL: 3 mL Prefilled Pen. Lantus® 100IU/mL: 3 mL cartridge and 10 mL Vial. 1 mL contains 3.6378 mg insulin glargine I.P. corresponding to 100 IU human insulin. 10 mL Vial Excipients (per mL): 30 μg zinc, 2.7 mg m-cresol, 20 mg glycerol 85%, 20 μg polysorbate 20, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide for pH adjustment, and water for injection. Cartridge Excipients (per mL): 30 μg zinc, 2.7 mg m-cresol, 20 mg glycerol 85%, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide for pH adjustment, and water for injection. The pH of the solution is 4.0.
strength: 100 IU/mL
adult_dosage: Lantus® is given subcutaneously once a day. It may be administered at any time during the day however at the same time every day. The desired blood glucose levels as well as the doses and timing of antidiabetic medications must be determined and adjusted individually. Dose adjustment may be required if the patient's weight, life-style changes, change in timing of insulin dose or other circumstances arise that increase susceptibility to hypo- or hyperglycemia. Lantus® is not the insulin of choice for the treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis. In basal bolus injection regimens usually 40 to 60% of the daily dose is administered as insulin glargine to cover basal insulin requirements. When changing from a treatment regimen with an intermediate or another long-acting insulin to a regimen with Lantus® the amount and timing of short-acting insulin or fast acting insulin analogue or of the dose of any oral antidiabetic drug may need to be adjusted. To reduce the risk of hypoglycemia when patients are transferred from once daily insulin glargine 300U/mL to once daily Lantus® the recommended initial Lantus® dose is 80% of the insulin glargine 300U/mL dose that is being discontinued. Lantus® must not be mixed with any other insulin. Lantus® must not be diluted. Lantus® is administered by subcutaneous tissue injection. It is not intended for intravenous administration. Injection sites within an injection area (abdomen, thigh or deltoid) must be rotated from one injection to the next to reduce the risk of lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. Do not inject into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis.
pediatric_dosage: Lantus® can be administered to children ≥ 2 years of age. Administration to children < 2 years has not been studied.
renal_dose_adjustment: In patients with renal impairment insulin requirements may be diminished due to reduced insulin metabolism. In the elderly progressive deterioration of renal function may lead to steady decrease in insulin requirements.
hepatic_dose_adjustment: In patients with severe hepatic impairment insulin requirements may be diminished due to reduced capacity for gluconeogenesis and reduced insulin metabolism.
side_effects: Hypoglycemia: The most frequent adverse reaction of insulin therapy — may occur if the insulin dose is too high in relation to the insulin requirement. Severe hypoglycemic attacks especially if recurrent may lead to neurological damage. Prolonged or severe hypoglycemic episodes may be life-threatening. Eye disorders: A marked change in glycemic control may cause temporary visual impairment due to temporary alteration in the turgidity and refractive index of the lens. Long-term improved glycemic control decreases the risk of progression of diabetic retinopathy. However intensification of insulin therapy with abrupt improvement in glycemic control may be associated with temporary worsening of diabetic retinopathy. Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders: Lipodystrophy may occur at the injection site and delay insulin absorption. In clinical studies lipohypertrophy was observed in 1 to 2% of patients and lipoatrophy was uncommon. Localized cutaneous amyloidosis at the injection site has occurred with insulins. Injection site and allergic reactions: In clinical studies injection site reactions were observed in 3 to 4% of patients (redness, pain, itching, hives, swelling, and inflammation). Immediate-type allergic reactions are rare — may be associated with generalised skin reactions, angiooedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension and shock and may be life-threatening. Insulin may cause sodium retention and oedema in rare cases.
pharmacokinetics: Absorption: After subcutaneous injection insulin glargine exhibits a slower and much more prolonged absorption and a lack of a peak in comparison to human NPH insulin. After subcutaneous injection of 0.3 IU/kg insulin glargine in diabetic patients a flat concentration-time profile has been demonstrated with a wide range of tmax values (between 1.5 and 22.5 hours) compared to NPH (2.5 to 10.0 hours). Distribution: When given intravenously the concentration profiles and the apparent elimination half-life of insulin glargine and human insulin were comparable. There were no relevant differences in serum insulin levels after abdominal, deltoid or thigh administration. Metabolism: Insulin glargine is rapidly metabolized at the carboxyl terminus of the Beta chain with formation of two active metabolites M1 (21AGly-insulin) and M2 (21A-Gly-des-30B-Thr-insulin). In plasma the principal circulating compound is the metabolite M1. Elimination: Not separately stated. The longer duration of action of insulin glargine is directly related to its slower rate of absorption and supports once daily administration. Special Populations: Information on the effect of age and gender on the pharmacokinetics of insulin glargine is unavailable. In children pharmacokinetics were similar to adults with no evidence of accumulation.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to insulin glargine or any of the excipients.
warnings_precautions: Insulin treatment requires constant alertness to the possibility of hyper- and hypoglycemia. Patients and their relatives must know what steps to take if hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia occurs or is suspected. Continuous rotation of the injection site must be performed to reduce the risk of developing lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis — potential risk of delayed insulin absorption and worsened glycemic control following insulin injections at sites with these reactions. A sudden change in the injection site to an unaffected area has been reported to result in hypoglycemia — blood glucose monitoring is recommended after the change. Hypoglycemia may occur — the time of occurrence depends on the action profile of the insulins used. Particular caution should be exercised and intensified blood glucose monitoring is advisable in patients in whom sequelae of hypoglycemic episodes might be of particular clinical relevance (e.g. patients with significant stenoses of the coronary arteries, patients with proliferative retinopathy). The warning symptoms of hypoglycemia may be changed, less pronounced or absent under certain conditions including: markedly improved glycemic control, hypoglycemia developing gradually, elderly patients, autonomic neuropathy, long history of diabetes, psychiatric illness, patients receiving concurrent treatment with certain other drugs. The prolonged effect of subcutaneous insulin glargine may delay recovery from hypoglycemia. In patients with renal impairment or severe hepatic impairment insulin requirements may be diminished. Intercurrent illness requires intensified metabolic monitoring — in many cases urine tests for ketones are indicated and often it is necessary to adjust the insulin dose. Lantus® cartridges should be used with Allstar® pen only.
drug_interactions: Substances that may increase the blood glucose lowering effect and susceptibility to hypoglycemia: oral antidiabetic products, ACE inhibitors, salicylates, disopyramide, fibrates, fluoxetine, MAO inhibitors, pentoxifylline, propoxyphene, sulfonamide antibiotics. Substances that may reduce the blood glucose lowering effect: corticosteroids, danazol, diazoxide, diuretics, sympathomimetic agents (such as epinephrine, salbutamol, terbutaline), glucagon, isoniazid, phenothiazine derivatives, somatropin, thyroid hormones, estrogens, progestogens (e.g. in oral contraceptives), protease inhibitors and atypical antipsychotic medications (e.g. olanzapine and clozapine). Beta-blockers, clonidine, lithium salts and alcohol may either potentiate or weaken the blood glucose lowering effect of insulin. Pentamidine may cause hypoglycemia which may sometimes be followed by hyperglycaemia. Under the influence of sympatholytic medicinal products such as beta-blockers, clonidine, guanethidine and reserpine the signs of adrenergic counter-regulation may be reduced or absent.
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: There are no randomized controlled clinical studies of the use of insulin glargine in pregnant women. A large number (more than 1000 retrospective and prospective pregnancy outcomes) of exposed pregnancies from Post Marketing Surveillance indicate no specific adverse effects of insulin glargine on pregnancy or on the health of the foetus and newborn child. A meta-analysis of eight observational clinical studies including 331 women using insulin glargine and 371 women using insulin NPH showed no significant differences in safety related maternal or neonatal outcomes. Animal studies with doses up to 6 to 40 times the human doses do not indicate direct harmful effects on the pregnancy. It is essential for patients with pre-existing or gestational diabetes to maintain good metabolic control throughout pregnancy. Lantus can be used during pregnancy if clinically needed. Insulin requirements may decrease during the first trimester and generally increase during the second and third trimesters. Immediately after delivery insulin requirements decline rapidly. Careful monitoring of glucose control is essential. Lactation: Lactating women may require adjustments in insulin dose and diet.
monitoring_parameters: Blood glucose monitoring is recommended for all patients with diabetes. Intensified blood glucose monitoring is advisable in patients at high risk of hypoglycemic episodes. Monitor for signs of hypoglycemia including symptoms of neuroglycopenia and adrenergic counter-regulation. Monitor injection sites for signs of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis. Blood glucose monitoring is recommended after change in injection site.
overdose_management: Symptoms: An excess of insulin relative to food intake, energy expenditure or both may lead to severe and sometimes prolonged and life-threatening hypoglycemia. Management: Mild episodes of hypoglycemia can usually be treated with oral carbohydrates. Adjustments in drug dosage, meal patterns or exercise may be needed. More severe episodes culminating in coma, seizure or neurologic impairment may be treated with intramuscular/subcutaneous glucagon or concentrated intravenous glucose. Sustained carbohydrate intake and observation may be necessary because hypoglycemia may recur after apparent clinical recovery.

clinical_evidence_summary: In clinical studies with insulin glargine the overall efficacy of once-daily insulin glargine on metabolic control was compared to that of once-daily and twice-daily NPH human insulin in open-label randomised active-control parallel studies of 2327 patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus and 1563 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. In general insulin glargine maintained or improved the level of glycemic control as measured by glycohemoglobin and fasting glucose. In addition fewer patients using insulin glargine reported a hypoglycemic episode compared to patients using NPH human insulin. ORIGIN Trial (Study 4032): The ORIGIN trial was an international multicenter randomized 2x2 factorial design study in 12537 participants. Participation for a median of approximately 6.2 years showed that treatment with Lantus did not alter the risk for cardiovascular outcomes, all-cause mortality or cancer when compared to standard glucose lowering therapy. In addition metabolic control was maintained at a lower level of glycemia with a decrease in the percentage of participants developing diabetes at a cost of a modest increase in hypoglycemia and weight gain.

indications: Treatment of resistant oedema where this is associated with secondary hyperaldosteronism, conditions include chronic congestive cardiac failure and hepatic cirrhosis. mechanism_of_action: Lasilactone® contains a short-acting diuretic and a long-acting aldosterone antagonist. This results in excretion of large amounts of sodium and chloride in urine. Frusemide increases the urinary excretion of potassium as well as water, sodium and chloride. Spironolactone: An aldosterone antagonist that competitively binds to aldosterone receptors in the distal tubule of the kidney. By blocking aldosterone it reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion. Since frusemide causes potassium loss and spironolactone causes potassium retention the two drugs have complementary potassium effects.

pediatric_dosage: NA

monitoring_parameters: Regular monitoring of serum sodium, potassium and creatinine. overdose_management: Signs and Symptoms: The clinical picture in acute or chronic overdose depends primarily on the extent and consequences of electrolyte and fluid loss — e.g. hypovolaemia, dehydration, haemoconcentration, cardiac arrhythmias due to excessive diuresis. Symptoms include severe hypotension (progressing to shock), acute renal failure, thrombosis, delirious states, flaccid paralysis, apathy and confusion. Management: No specific antidote is known. If ingestion has only just taken place attempts may be made to limit further systemic absorption of the active ingredient by measures such as gastric lavage or those designed to reduce absorption (e.g. activated charcoal). Clinically relevant disturbances in electrolyte and fluid balance must be corrected. Prevention and treatment of serious complications may necessitate general and specific intensive medical monitoring and therapeutic measures.

mechanism_of_action: Alemtuzumab is a humanized anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody. CD52 is a cell surface antigen present on T and B lymphocytes as well as NK cells, monocytes, and macrophages. By binding to CD52 alemtuzumab causes lysis of CD52-bearing cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-mediated lysis. This leads to depletion of T and B lymphocytes. The repopulation of lymphocytes following treatment is thought to result in immune reconstitution that resets the aberrant immune response in MS. The immunomodulatory mechanism by which alemtuzumab exerts its therapeutic effects in MS is not fully understood but is thought to involve re-establishment of immune tolerance.

Acquired hemophilia A: Patients typically present with spontaneous subcutaneous hematomas and extensive bruising. A coagulopathy panel including aPTT must be obtained in all patients who present with such symptoms. Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura: Serious events of ITP have been observed in 1% of patients. Complete blood counts (CBC) with differential should be obtained prior to initiation of treatment and at monthly intervals thereafter until 48 months after the last infusion. Nephropathies: Serum creatinine levels and urinalysis with cell counts should be obtained prior to initiation of treatment and at monthly intervals thereafter until 48 months after the last infusion. Thyroid Disorders: Autoimmune thyroid disorders including hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism observed in 36.8% of patients. Thyroid function tests such as TSH levels should be obtained prior to initiation of treatment and every 3 months thereafter until 48 months after the last infusion. Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH): Liver function tests should be performed before initial treatment and at monthly intervals until at least 48 months after the last infusion. Infusion-associated Reactions (IARs): Observation for infusion reactions is recommended during and for at least 2 hours after LEMTRADA infusion. Resources for management of anaphylaxis or serious reactions should be available. Avalglucosidase alfa has a 15-fold increase in mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) moieties compared with alglucosidase alfa. Increasing the level of bis-M6P on rhGAA provides a mechanism to drive uptake into the diaphragm and other skeletal muscle via the cation-independent M6P receptor, where it can degrade glycogen and ameliorate tissue damage.

indications: Secondary prevention of atherothrombotic events in: (1) Recent MI, Recent Stroke or Established Peripheral Arterial Disease — reduces the rate of new ischemic stroke (fatal or not), new MI (fatal or not), and other vascular death. (2) Acute Coronary Syndrome (unstable angina/non-Q-wave MI, ST-elevation AMI) — decreases the rate of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke as well as rate of cardiovascular death, MI, stroke or refractory ischemia. (3) Patients with moderate to high-risk Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) or minor Ischemic Stroke (IS) within 24 hours — in combination with ASA. (4) Atrial Fibrillation — for patients who cannot take VKA therapy, clopidogrel is indicated in combination with ASA for the prevention of atherothrombotic and thromboembolic events including stroke.
mechanism_of_action: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that is metabolized by CYP2C19 (and to a lesser extent CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2B6) to an active thiol metabolite. The active metabolite selectively inhibits the binding of adenosine diphosphate (ADP) to its platelet P2Y12 receptor and the subsequent ADP-mediated activation of the glycoprotein GPIIb/IIIa complex, thereby inhibiting platelet aggregation. The binding is irreversible — platelets are affected for their lifetime (7-10 days). Platelet aggregation induced by agonists other than ADP is also inhibited by blocking the amplification of platelet activation by released ADP. Because the active metabolite is formed by CYP2C19 enzymes, use of drugs that inhibit the activity of this enzyme would be expected to result in reduced drug levels of the active metabolite and reduced platelet inhibition (CYP2C19 poor metabolizers).

side_effects: Bleeding including life-threatening and fatal bleeding is the most commonly reported adverse reaction. Gastrointestinal bleeding, other bleeding disorders including purpura/bruising, epistaxis, haematoma, haematuria and eye bleeding (mainly conjunctival). Other common adverse reactions: dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea. Uncommon: Dizziness, paraesthesia, headache, gastric ulcer and duodenal ulcer, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, constipation, rash, pruritus. Rare: Vertigo, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), severe thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis. pharmacokinetics: Absorption: After single and repeated oral doses of 75 mg per day clopidogrel is rapidly absorbed with peak plasma levels occurring approximately 45 minutes after dosing. The mean absolute bioavailability is low (approximately 50%) due to first-pass metabolism. The major circulating metabolite is the carboxylic acid derivative which represents about 85% of the circulating drug-related compounds in plasma. The active thiol metabolite accounts for approximately 2% of the circulating drug-related compounds. The active metabolite is formed mainly by CYP2C19 with contributions from CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2B6. Distribution: Clopidogrel and its main carboxylic acid metabolite bind reversibly to human plasma proteins in vitro (98% and 94% respectively). Metabolism: Clopidogrel is extensively metabolized by the liver. In vitro and in vivo studies show that CYP2C19 is involved in the formation of both the active metabolite and of 2-oxo-clopidogrel. The pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the active metabolite are affected by polymorphisms of the CYP2C19 gene. In patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers clopidogrel at recommended doses forms less of the active metabolite and has a smaller effect on platelet function. Elimination: After oral dosing of 14C-labeled clopidogrel approximately 50% was excreted in the urine and approximately 46% in the feces in the 120-hour interval after dosing. The elimination half-life of the main carboxylic acid metabolite was 8 hours after single and repeated administration.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the drug substance or any component of the product. Active pathological bleeding such as peptic ulcer or intracranial haemorrhage.
warnings_precautions: Bleeding and haematological disorders: Due to the risk of bleeding, blood cell count determination should be undertaken. Concomitant administration of warfarin with clopidogrel should be undertaken with caution because of the increased risk of bleeding. Clopidogrel should be used with caution in patients who may be at risk of increased bleeding from trauma, surgery or other pathological conditions and in patients receiving treatment with ASA, heparin, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, NSAIDs, SSRIs or CYP2C19 strong inducers. Due to the increased risk of hemorrhage triple antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel + aspirin + dipyridamole) for stroke secondary prevention is not recommended. If a patient is to undergo elective surgery and an antiplatelet effect is not desired clopidogrel should be discontinued 5 to 7 days prior to surgery. Clopidogrel prolongs bleeding time — use with caution in patients with lesions with a propensity to bleed. The use of clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose is not recommended in patients with non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome and ≥75 years of age due to increased bleeding risk. Recent ischemic stroke: Dual antiplatelet therapy should be started no later than 24 hours after the event onset. There is no data to support the use of dual antiplatelet therapy in patients for whom treatment with carotid endarterectomy or intravascular thrombectomy is indicated or in patients planned for thrombolysis or anticoagulant therapy. Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP): Has been reported very rarely following the use of clopidogrel — potentially fatal condition requiring prompt treatment including plasmapheresis. Acquired haemophilia: Has been reported following use of clopidogrel — patients with confirmed diagnosis should be managed by specialists and clopidogrel should be discontinued. CYP2C19 poor metabolizers: Clopidogrel at recommended doses forms less of the active metabolite and has a smaller effect on platelet function — higher cardiovascular event rates may result. Consider use of higher clopidogrel doses in poor metabolizers. Cross-reactivity among thienopyridines: Patients should be evaluated for history of hypersensitivity to another thienopyridine — cross-reactivity has been reported. Renal impairment: Use with caution in patients with severe renal impairment. Hepatic impairment: Use with caution in patients with severe hepatic disease. Excipients: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
drug_interactions: Drugs associated with bleeding risk: There is an increased risk of bleeding due to the potential additive effect — concomitant administration should be undertaken with caution. Thrombolytics, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, injectable anticoagulants, oral anticoagulants (warfarin), ASA, NSAIDs, SSRIs should all be used with caution. Inhibitors of CYP2C19: Since clopidogrel is metabolized to its active metabolite partly by CYP2C19 use of drugs that inhibit the activity of this enzyme would be expected to result in reduced drug levels of the active metabolite. Concomitant use of strong or moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole) should be discouraged. If a PPI is to be used concomitantly with clopidogrel consider using one with less CYP2C19 inhibitory activity such as pantoprazole. Clopidogrel with omeprazole (80 mg) decreased the exposure to the active metabolite by 45% (Day 1) and 40% (Day 5) and diminished mean IPA by 39% (24 hours) and 21% (Day 5). Inducers of CYP2C19: Rifampicin strongly induces CYP2C19 resulting in increased clopidogrel active metabolite levels and platelet inhibition — may potentiate the risk of bleeding, concomitant use should be discouraged. CYP2C8 substrate drugs: Clopidogrel has been shown to increase repaglinide exposure — concomitant administration of clopidogrel and drugs primarily cleared by CYP2C8 metabolism (e.g. repaglinide, paclitaxel) should be undertaken with caution. Rosuvastatin: Clopidogrel has been shown to increase rosuvastatin exposure by 2-fold (AUC) and 1.3-fold (Cmax) after administration of a 300 mg clopidogrel dose. Opioid agonists: Co-administration has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel — consider use of a parenteral antiplatelet agent in ACS patients requiring co-administration of morphine or other opioid agonists. No clinically significant pharmacodynamic interactions were observed with atenolol, nifedipine, phenobarbital, oestrogen, digoxin, theophylline or antacids.
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: Reproduction studies performed in rats and rabbits have revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the foetus due to clopidogrel. There are however no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of a human response this drug should not be used during pregnancy unless in the opinion of the physician there is a clear need. Lactation: Studies in rats have shown that clopidogrel and/or its metabolites are excreted in the milk. It is not known whether this drug is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or to discontinue the drug. Fertility: No information available.
monitoring_parameters: Blood cell count determination if unusual bleeding symptoms arise during the course of treatment. INR monitoring if co-administered with warfarin. Monitoring for signs and symptoms of bleeding. Consider CYP2C19 genotype testing as an aid in determining therapeutic strategy. Monitor for cross-reactivity symptoms in patients with history of thienopyridine hypersensitivity. Monitor blood pressure. Monitor for signs of TTP (thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, neurological findings, renal dysfunction, fever).
overdose_management: Not specifically stated in the PI, however in cases of overdose symptomatic and supportive treatment should be given. Clopidogrel prolongs the bleeding time — bleeding time may be of concern in overdose situations.

mechanism_of_action: Mucopolysaccharide storage disorders are caused by the deficiency of specific lysosomal enzymes required for the catabolism of glycosaminoglycans (GAG). Mucopolysaccharidosis I (MPS I) is characterized by the deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase, a lysosomal hydrolase which catalyzes the hydrolysis of terminal alpha-L-iduronic acid residues of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. Reduced or absent alpha-L-iduronidase activity results in the accumulation of the GAG substrates, dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, throughout the body and leads to widespread cellular, tissue, and organ dysfunction. The rationale of ALDURAZYME therapy in MPS I is to provide exogenous enzyme for uptake into lysosomes and increase the catabolism of GAG. ALDURAZYME uptake by cells into lysosomes is most likely mediated by the mannose-6-phosphate-terminated oligosaccharide chains of laronidase binding to specific mannose-6-phosphate receptors. Because many proteins in the blood are restricted from entry into the CNS by the blood brain barrier, effects of intravenously administered ALDURAZYME on cells within the CNS cannot be inferred from activity in sites outside the CNS.

The initial infusion rate is 10 mcg/kg/hr and may be increased every 15 minutes to a maximum infusion rate of 200 mcg/kg/hr. The total infusion volume should be administered over approximately 3 to 4 hours. If one or more doses are missed, restart ALDURAZYME treatment as soon as possible and maintain the 1-week interval between infusions. Do not double a dose to compensate for a missed dose. Premedication: Prior to ALDURAZYME administration consider premedicating with antihistamines, with or without antipyretics, 60 minutes before the start of infusion.
pediatric_dosage: The safety and effectiveness of ALDURAZYME have been established for the treatment of pediatric patients with MPS I. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients 6 months to 5 years of age were similar to those 6 to 18 years of age and adults.
renal_dose_adjustment: No formal dose adjustment recommended. Clinical monitoring is advised.
hepatic_dose_adjustment: No formal dose adjustment recommended in the absence of clinical studies. Caution should be used in hepatically impaired patients.
side_effects: Most common adverse reactions in clinical trials were infusion reactions. Serious adverse reactions included anaphylactic and hypersensitivity reactions. Most common adverse reactions (occurring in at least 2 patients more in the ALDURAZYME group than placebo): Injection site reaction, upper respiratory tract infection, thrombocytopenia, corneal opacity, chest pain, face edema, gravitational edema, injection site pain, hyperbilirubinemia, abscess, hyperreflexia, paresthesia, rash, hypotension, poor venous access. Additional adverse reactions in open-label extension: flushing (11%), pyrexia (11%), headache (9%), abdominal pain or discomfort (9%), injection site reaction (9%), nausea (7%), diarrhea (7%), feeling hot or cold (7%), vomiting (4%), pruritus (4%), arthralgia (4%), urticaria (4%), back pain, musculoskeletal pain, rash (13%). Postmarketing severe reactions including laryngeal edema, cardiorespiratory arrest, respiratory failure, cardiac failure, pneumonia, fatigue, peripheral edema, erythema, cyanosis. Anaphylactic shock and associated death have been reported.
contraindications: None.
warnings_precautions: Hypersensitivity Reactions Including Anaphylaxis: Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis have been reported during or up to 3 hours after ALDURAZYME infusions, approximately 1% were severe or serious. Appropriate medical monitoring and support measures including cardiopulmonary resuscitation equipment should be readily available when ALDURAZYME is administered. If severe hypersensitivity reaction occurs discontinue ALDURAZYME immediately and initiate appropriate medical treatment. Consider risks and benefits of re-administering ALDURAZYME following severe hypersensitivity reactions. Patients with a history of severe hypersensitivity reactions may be rechallenged using slower infusion rates with desensitization measures as appropriate. Acute Respiratory Complications: One patient with acute bronchitis and hypoxia experienced increased tachypnea during the first infusion and subsequently died from respiratory arrest. Patients with an acute febrile or respiratory illness at the time of ALDURAZYME infusion may be at greater risk for infusion reactions. Consider evaluating airway patency prior to initiation of treatment. Sleep apnea is common in MPS I patients — patients using supplemental oxygen or CPAP should have these treatments readily available during infusion. Acute Cardiorespiratory Failure: Cases of acute cardiorespiratory failure have been reported postmarketing. Patients susceptible to fluid overload, or patients with acute underlying respiratory illness or compromised cardiac and/or respiratory function may be at increased risk. Consider a decreased total infusion volume and infusion rate in these patients. Infusion-Associated Reactions (IARs): ALDURAZYME may cause IARs. Prior to administration consider pre-medicating with antihistamines, with or without antipyretics 60 minutes before the start of infusion to reduce the risk of IARs.
drug_interactions: None (see section Drug Interactions).
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: Available data from the MPS I Registry pregnancy sub-registry, published case reports and global pharmacovigilance database with ALDURAZYME use in more than 30 pregnant women have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. The continuation of treatment for MPS I during pregnancy should be individualized to the pregnant woman. No evidence of fetal harm has been observed in rats when laronidase was administered during organogenesis at doses up to 6.2 times the recommended human dose. Lactation: Available information from one mother-infant pair are insufficient to evaluate the presence or absence of laronidase in human milk. No adverse effects have been reported in breastfed infants in postmarketing cases. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need for ALDURAZYME.
monitoring_parameters: Monitor for signs and symptoms of hypersensitivity reactions during and for at least 2 hours after each infusion. Monitor vital signs and clinical status during infusion. For IOPD patients — IgG antibody titre monitoring based on clinical phenotype (every 3 months during first year). Periodic urinalysis for patients with high IgG antibody titres. Monitor for signs of immune-mediated reactions involving skin and other organs.
overdose_management: Overdose: None described. In the event of overdose reduce infusion rate or temporarily interrupt. There is no known specific antidote for laronidase overdose.
clinical_evidence_summary: Study 1 (NCT00912925): A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study in 45 patients with MPS I. Patients received ALDURAZYME 0.58 mg/kg IV once weekly or placebo for 26 weeks. After 26 weeks patients treated with ALDURAZYME showed improvement in percent predicted FVC (mean change +1% vs -3% for placebo, difference 4, median difference 2 [0.4-7] p=0.02) and in 6-minute walk test (mean change +20m vs -18m, median difference 39 (-2 to 79) p=0.07). Liver size and urinary GAG levels decreased in ALDURAZYME-treated patients compared to placebo. Study 3: A 52-week open-label uncontrolled study in 20 MPS I patients 6 months to 5 years of age. Safety and effectiveness similar to pediatric patients 6 to 18 years and adults.

mechanism_of_action: Insulin glulisine is a recombinant human insulin analogue that has been shown to be equipotent to human insulin. One unit of Apidra® has the same glucose-lowering effect as one unit of regular human insulin. After subcutaneous administration it has a more rapid onset and a shorter duration of action. Insulin glulisine differs from human insulin in that the amino acid asparagine at position B3 is replaced by lysine and the lysine in position B29 is replaced by glutamic acid. The primary activity of insulin — including insulin glulisine — is regulation of glucose metabolism. Insulin and its analogues lower blood glucose levels by stimulating peripheral glucose uptake especially by skeletal muscle and fat and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production.

adult_dosage: Apidra® should be given by subcutaneous injection within 15 minutes before a meal or within 20 minutes after starting a meal. The dosage of Apidra® should be individualized and determined based on the physician's advice in accordance with the needs of the patient. Apidra® should normally be used in regimens that include a longer-acting insulin or basal insulin analogue. Blood glucose monitoring is recommended for all patients with diabetes. Apidra® is intended for subcutaneous administration by injection or by external infusion pump. Apidra® can also be administered intravenously. Apidra® should be administered subcutaneously either by injection in the abdominal wall, the thigh or deltoid or by continuous subcutaneous infusion in the abdominal wall. Injection sites and infusion sites within an injection area must be rotated from one injection to the next to reduce the risk of lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. Mixing: Apidra® can be mixed with NPH human insulin — Apidra® should be drawn into the syringe first and injection made immediately after mixing. Mixtures should not be administered intravenously. For intravenous use Apidra® should be used at a concentration of 1 unit/mL insulin glulisine in infusion systems with the infusion fluid sterile 0.9% sodium chloride solution. side_effects: Hypoglycemia — the most frequent adverse reaction of insulin therapy. Local allergy: redness, swelling and itching at the site of insulin injection. Systemic allergic reactions to insulin (including insulin glulisine) may be associated with rash over the whole body, shortness of breath, wheezing, reduction of blood pressure, rapid pulse, or sweating. Severe cases of generalised allergy including anaphylactic reaction may be life threatening. Lipodystrophy at the injection site and delay insulin absorption. Localized cutaneous amyloidosis at the injection site has occurred with insulins. Hyperglycemia has been reported with repeated insulin injections into areas of localized cutaneous amyloidosis, hypoglycemia with sudden change to unaffected injection site. Medication errors in which other insulins, particularly long-acting insulins, have been accidentally administered instead of insulin glulisine.

If refrigeration not possible, keep unrefrigerated up to 28 days away from direct heat and light as long as temperature is not greater than 25°C (77°F). Once a cartridge is placed in a pen it must not be put in a refrigerator.

Distribution: Volume of distribution 13 L. Metabolism: Metabolized by the liver. Elimination: Mean half-life approximately 13 minutes, duration of action 1 to 2.5 hours after subcutaneous injection. Changes in insulin strength, manufacturer, type, species or method of manufacture may result in the need for a change in dosage. Concomitant oral antidiabetic treatment may need to be adjusted. Insulin requirements may be altered during intercurrent conditions such as illness, emotional disturbances, or stress. Patients must be instructed to perform continuous rotation of the injection site to reduce the risk of developing lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. There is a potential risk of delayed insulin absorption and worsened glycemic control following insulin injections at sites with these reactions. A sudden change in the injection site to an unaffected area has been reported to result in hypoglycemia. Blood glucose monitoring is recommended after the change in the injection site, and dose adjustment of antidiabetic medications may be considered. Under certain conditions the warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia may be changed, less pronounced or absent (if glycaemic control is markedly improved, hypoglycaemia developing gradually, elderly patients, where an autonomic neuropathy is present, in patients with a long history of diabetes, in patients receiving concurrent treatment with certain drugs). Apidra® cartridges should only be used with AllStar® which delivers Apidra® in 1-unit dose increments. Continuous subcutaneous infusion pump: malfunction may rapidly lead to hyperglycaemia, ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis. Patients using CSII must be trained to administer insulin by injection and have alternate insulin delivery system available.
drug_interactions: Substances that may enhance the blood-glucose-lowering effect: oral antidiabetic agents, ACE inhibitors, disopyramide, fibrates, fluoxetine, MAO inhibitors, pentoxifylline, propoxyphene, salicylates and sulfonamide antibiotics. Substances that may reduce the blood-glucose-lowering effect: corticosteroids, danazol, diazoxide, diuretics, glucagon, isoniazid, oestrogens and progestogens, phenothiazine derivatives, somatropin, sympathomimetic agents, thyroid hormones, protease inhibitors and atypical antipsychotic medications (e.g. olanzapine and clozapine). Beta-blockers, clonidine, lithium salts or alcohol may either potentiate or weaken the blood glucose lowering effect of insulin. Pentamidine may cause hypoglycaemia followed by hyperglycaemia. Under the influence of sympatholytic medicinal products (beta-blockers, clonidine, guanethidine and reserpine) the signs of adrenergic counter-regulation may be reduced or absent.
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: There are no well-controlled clinical studies of the use of Apidra® in pregnant women. A limited amount of data on pregnant women (less than 300 pregnancy outcomes reported) exposed to marketed insulin glulisine indicates no safety issues in use during pregnancy or on the foetus and newborn child. It is essential for patients with diabetes to maintain good metabolic control before conception and throughout pregnancy. Insulin requirements may decrease during the first trimester, generally increase during the second and third trimesters and rapidly decline after delivery. Careful monitoring of glucose control is essential. Lactation: It is unknown whether Apidra® is excreted in human milk. Lactating women may require adjustments in insulin dose and diet.
monitoring_parameters: Blood glucose monitoring. Monitor injection sites for lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis. Monitor blood glucose after change in injection site.
overdose_management: Hypoglycemia: Mild/moderate episodes can usually be treated with oral carbohydrates. Severe episodes with coma, seizure or neurologic impairment may be treated with intramuscular/subcutaneous glucagon or concentrated intravenous glucose. Sustained carbohydrate intake and observation may be necessary because hypoglycaemia may recur after apparent clinical recovery.

indications: Treatment of patients with relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (MS).
mechanism_of_action: Teriflunomide is an immunomodulatory agent with anti-inflammatory properties that selectively and reversibly inhibits the mitochondrial enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHO-DH), required for the de novo pyrimidine synthesis. As a consequence teriflunomide blocks the proliferation of stimulated lymphocytes which need de novo synthesis of pyrimidine to expand. The exact mechanism by which teriflunomide exerts its therapeutic effect in MS is not fully understood but may include reduced number of activated lymphocytes in the central nervous system (CNS). Teriflunomide is an oral de novo pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor of the DHO-DH enzyme with the chemical name (Z)-2-Cyano-3-hydroxy-but-2-enoic acid-(4-trifluoromethylphenyl)-amide.
composition: Active ingredient: Teriflunomide 14 mg. Excipients: lactose monohydrate, corn starch, hydroxypropylcellulose, microcrystalline cellulose, sodium starch glycolate, and magnesium stearate. strength: 14 mg
adult_dosage: The recommended dose of AUBAGIO® is 14 mg orally once daily. AUBAGIO® can be taken with or without food. Treatment should be monitored by physician. If ALT elevation confirmed >3 times ULN discontinue and start accelerated elimination procedure.
pediatric_dosage: NA
renal_dose_adjustment: No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with severe renal impairment.
hepatic_dose_adjustment: No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment. Teriflunomide is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment.
side_effects: Clinical trial adverse reactions (≥1% and ≥1% higher than placebo): Influenza, sinusitis, gastroenteritis viral, neutropenia, headache, paraesthesia, palpitations, hypertension, diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain upper, toothache, alopecia, rash, arthralgia, musculoskeletal pain, myalgia, menorrhagia, alanine aminotransferase increased, aspartate aminotransferase increased, gamma-glutamyltransferase increased, weight decreased, neutrophil count decreased, blood creatine phosphokinase increased, white blood cell count decreased, polyneuropathy. Post-marketing adverse reactions: Hypersensitivity reactions (including anaphylaxis and angioedema), severe skin reactions including toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), psoriasis (including pustular psoriasis and nail psoriasis), nail disorders, interstitial lung disease (ILD), pulmonary hypertension, stomatitis (such as aphthous or ulcerative), pancreatitis, colitis, drug-induced liver injury (DILI).

pharmacokinetics: Absorption: After oral administration teriflunomide is well absorbed with a mean time to peak plasma concentration (tmax) of approximately 1 to 4 hours. No effect of food on pharmacokinetics. Bioavailability approximately 100%. Distribution: Teriflunomide has a low volume of distribution and is highly protein-bound (>99%). Metabolism: The primary biotransformation pathway for teriflunomide is hydrolysis with oxidation being a minor pathway with limited involvement of CYP enzymes. Elimination: Very long half-life due to enterohepatic recycling — mean plasma half-life is approximately 18–19 days at steady state. Without the accelerated elimination procedure on average it takes 8 months to reach plasma concentrations ≤0.02 μg/mL, however due to individual variation it may take up to 2 years. Accelerated elimination procedure: Administration of activated charcoal 50 g every 12 hours for 11 days or cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days can be used to quickly decrease plasma levels.
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to teriflunomide, leflunomide or to any of the inactive ingredients, severe hepatic impairment, pregnant women, or women of childbearing potential who are not using reliable contraception, during treatment with teriflunomide and thereafter as long as its plasma levels are above 0.02 mg/l.
warnings_precautions: Hepatic Effects: Elevations of liver enzymes have been observed. Obtain serum transaminase and bilirubin levels within 6 months before initiation. Monitor ALT levels at least monthly for six months after starting. Consider monitoring when AUBAGIO® is given with other potentially hepatotoxic drugs. Consider discontinuing AUBAGIO® if serum transaminase increase greater than three times ULN is confirmed. If liver injury is suspected to be AUBAGIO®-induced discontinue teriflunomide and start an accelerated elimination procedure and monitor liver tests weekly until normalized. Pregnancy and Women of Childbearing Potential: Women of childbearing potential must use effective contraception. If AUBAGIO® is stopped, women should continue contraception until teriflunomide plasma concentrations have been checked to be ≤0.02 μg/mL or lower. An accelerated elimination procedure can be used to quickly decrease plasma concentration. Blood Pressure: Check blood pressure before start and periodically thereafter. Infections: If patient develops a serious infection consider suspending treatment. Patients with active acute or chronic infections should not start treatment until infection is resolved. Not recommended with severe immunodeficiency, bone marrow disease, or severe uncontrolled infections. Tuberculosis screening before therapy. Respiratory Effects: Interstitial lung disease reported postmarketing — new onset or worsening pulmonary symptoms may be reason for discontinuation. Hematologic Effects: Mean decrease in WBC count of approximately 15% and platelet count of approximately 10%. Blood cell count should be available before initiation. Severe skin reactions (SCARs): SJS, TEN, DRESS reported. If skin/mucosal reactions are observed discontinue teriflunomide immediately and initiate accelerated elimination procedure. Peripheral Neuropathy: If patient develops confirmed peripheral neuropathy consider discontinuing AUBAGIO® and performing the accelerated elimination procedure. Concomitant Immunosuppressive/Immunomodulating Therapies: Co-administration with leflunomide is not recommended. Elimination Procedure: Teriflunomide is eliminated slowly from plasma — accelerated elimination with cholestyramine or activated charcoal can be used when desired.
drug_interactions: Teriflunomide is a substrate of BCRP — BCRP inhibitors (cyclosporine, eltrombopag, gefitinib) may increase exposure. Teriflunomide is an inhibitor of CYP2C8 in vivo — monitoring recommended for substrates metabolized by CYP2C8 (repaglinide, paclitaxel, pioglitazone, rosiglitazone). Warfarin: 25% decrease in peak INR observed — close INR follow-up recommended. Oral contraceptives: increase in mean ethinylestradiol Cmax and AUC (1.58- and 1.54-fold respectively) and levonorgestrel Cmax and AUC (1.33- and 1.41-fold respectively) — consideration should be given to the type or dose of oral contraceptives used. CYP1A2 substrates (duloxetine, alosetron, theophylline, tizanidine): teriflunomide is a weak inducer of CYP1A2 — use with caution. OAT3 substrates (cefaclor, penicillin G, ciprofloxacin, indomethacin, ketoprofen, furosemide, cimetidine, methotrexate, zidovudine): teriflunomide is an inhibitor of OAT3 — caution should be observed. BCRP and OATP1B1/B3 substrates (rosuvastatin): do not exceed 10 mg once daily. For other BCRP substrates (methotrexate, topotecan, sulfasalazine, daunorubicin, doxorubicin) and OATP family (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) concomitant administration should be undertaken with caution.
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: Based on animal studies AUBAGIO® may increase the risk of fetal death or teratogenic effects when administered to pregnant women. Teriflunomide is contraindicated in pregnancy. Prospectively reported data from >150 pregnancies treated with teriflunomide and >300 pregnancies treated with leflunomide have not demonstrated an increased rate of congenital malformations or miscarriage following teriflunomide exposure in the early first trimester when followed by an accelerated elimination procedure. Females: use effective contraception during treatment and after stopping until plasma concentrations are ≤0.02 μg/mL. Males: The risk of male-mediated embryo-fetal toxicity is considered low, however effective contraception is advised. Lactation: Animal studies have shown excretion of teriflunomide in breast milk. It is not known whether this drug is excreted in human milk. A decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or to discontinue the drug.
monitoring_parameters: Monitor serum transaminase and bilirubin before initiation and at least monthly for 6 months. Blood cell count before initiation and as clinically indicated. Blood pressure before start and periodically. TSH level monitoring if thyroid dysfunction is suspected. Monitor for signs of peripheral neuropathy. Monitor for signs of serious infections.
overdose_management: There is no experience regarding teriflunomide overdose or intoxication in humans. Teriflunomide 70 mg daily up to 14 days was well tolerated by healthy subjects. In the event of relevant overdose or toxicity cholestyramine or activated charcoal is recommended to accelerate elimination.

clinical_evidence_summary: Study 1 (EFC6049/TEMSO): A double-blind placebo-controlled study in 1088 patients with RMS treated with teriflunomide 7 mg, 14 mg or placebo over 108 weeks. The ARR was significantly reduced in both teriflunomide groups compared to placebo. The risk of disability progression sustained for 12 weeks was statistically significantly reduced only in the teriflunomide 14 mg group compared to placebo. Study 2 (EFC10891/TOWER): Further confirmatory phase 3 study also demonstrated reduction in ARR with teriflunomide 14 mg. Long term follow-up from the TEMSO long term extension safety study also available.

symptoms: Elevated blood pressure (hypertension), headache, dizziness, tickling cough, oedema, flushing, palpitations
indications: For the treatment of hypertension.
mechanism_of_action: Ramipril: Ramiprilat, the active metabolite of the prodrug ramipril, inhibits the enzyme dipeptidylcarboxypeptidase I (angiotensin-converting enzyme, kininase II). In plasma and tissue this enzyme catalyses the conversion of angiotensin I to the active vasoconstrictor substance angiotensin II as well as the breakdown of the active vasodilator bradykinin. Reduced angiotensin II formation and inhibition of bradykinin breakdown lead to vasodilation. Since angiotensin II also stimulates the release of aldosterone ramiprilat causes a reduction in aldosterone secretion. Amlodipine: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. It inhibits the transmembrane influx of calcium ions into cardiac and vascular smooth muscle without affecting serum calcium concentrations. Direct relaxation of vascular smooth muscle forms the basis of the antihypertensive action.
composition: Cardace® am 10: Each uncoated tablet contains Ramipril IP 10.0 mg + Amlodipine Besylate IP equivalent to Amlodipine 5.0 mg. Cardace® am 5: Each uncoated tablet contains Ramipril IP 5.0 mg + Amlodipine Besylate IP equivalent to Amlodipine 5.0 mg. Cardace® am 2.5: Each uncoated tablet contains Ramipril IP 2.5 mg + Amlodipine Besylate IP equivalent to Amlodipine 5.0 mg.
strength: Ramipril 2.5 mg or 5 mg or 10 mg + Amlodipine 5 mg
adult_dosage: Recommended initial dose is one tablet of Cardace® am 2.5mg/5mg once daily. Depending on patient's response the dose may be increased. Cardace® am 5mg/5mg or Cardace® am 10mg/5mg may be used for higher dosing. It is recommended that dose increase should be done at intervals of 2 or 3 weeks. Maximum permitted daily dose of ramipril is 10 mg and the maximum recommended daily dose of amlodipine is up to 10 mg. Cardace® am must be swallowed with sufficient amount of liquid (approx. half glass). The tablet must not be chewed or crushed.
pediatric_dosage: Clinical studies of CARDACE® am did not include patients over 65 years old. CARDACE® am should be used with caution in patients aged over 65 years. Initial doses should be lower and subsequent dose titration should be more gradual for elderly patients.
renal_dose_adjustment: Amlodipine may be used in such patients at normal doses. Changes in amlodipine plasma concentrations are not correlated with degree of renal impairment. Amlodipine is not dialyzable. For Ramipril: Insufficient experience has been gained in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 20 ml/min per 1.73 m² body surface area) and in dialysis patients.
hepatic_dose_adjustment: For Amlodipine: The half-life of amlodipine is prolonged and AUC values are higher in patients with impaired liver function — initiate at lower end of dosing range, caution should be used, slow dose titration and careful monitoring may be required in patients with severe hepatic impairment. For Ramipril: Response to treatment with ramipril may be either increased or reduced. In patients with severe liver cirrhosis with oedema and/or ascites the renin angiotensin system may be significantly activated.
side_effects: Ramipril — Common: Blood potassium increased, headache, dizziness, hypotension, orthostatic blood pressure decreased, syncope, non-productive tickling cough, bronchitis, sinusitis, dyspnoea, gastrointestinal inflammation, digestive disturbances, abdominal discomfort, dyspepsia, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, rash in particular maculo-papular, muscle spasms, myalgia, chest pain, fatigue. Uncommon: Eosinophilia, depressed mood, anxiety, nervousness, restlessness, sleep disorder, confusional state, disturbance in attention, vertigo, paraesthesia, ageusia, dysgeusia, visual disturbance including blurred vision, conjunctivitis, hearing impaired, tinnitus, myocardial ischemia including angina pectoris or myocardial infarction, tachycardia, arrhythmia, palpitations, oedema peripheral, flushing, bronchospasm including asthma aggravated, nasal congestion, vomiting, aphtous stomatitis, glossitis, diarrhoea, abdominal pain upper, dry mouth, renal impairment including renal failure acute, blood urea increased, blood creatinine increased, angioedema, dermatitis psoriasiform, hyperhidrosis, pruritus, alopecia, myalgia, arthralgia, proteinuria increased. Rare: White blood cell count decreased, red blood cell count decreased, haemoglobin decreased, platelet count decreased, bone marrow failure, haemolytic anaemia, anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions, toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme. Amlodipine — Very common: Oedema. Common: Somnolence, dizziness, headache, visual disturbance including diplopia, palpitations, flushing, dyspnoea, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspepsia, altered bowel habits, ankle swelling, muscle cramps, fatigue, asthenia, impotence, gynaecomastia.
contraindications: Cardace® am must not be used in patients with hypersensitivity to ramipril, amlodipine, other ACE inhibitors, dihydropyridine derivatives or to any of the excipients, patients with a history of angioedema, concomitantly with sacubitril/valsartan therapy, patients with haemodynamically relevant renal artery stenosis bilateral or unilateral in the single kidney, patients with hypotensive or haemodynamically unstable states, with aliskiren-containing medicines in patients with diabetes or with moderate to severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <60 ml/min), with angiotensin II receptor antagonists (AIIRAs) in patients with diabetic nephropathy, during pregnancy. For Amlodipine: patients with severe hypotension, patients with shock (including cardiogenic shock), patients with obstruction of the outflow tract of the left ventricle (e.g. high grade aortic stenosis), patients with haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.
warnings_precautions: Ramipril: Angioedema of the face, extremities, lips, tongue, glottis or larynx has been reported — necessitates immediate discontinuation. Emergency treatment includes immediate administration of epinephrine. An increased risk of angioedema is possible with concomitant use of other drugs which may cause angioedema. Desensitization therapy: The likelihood and severity of anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions to insect venoma is increased under ACE inhibition. Dual blockade of RAAS — not recommended, contraindicated in patients with diabetes or renal impairment. Patients with hyper-stimulated renin angiotensin system are at risk of an acute pronounced fall in blood pressure and deterioration of renal function. Monitoring of renal function particularly in the initial weeks of treatment is recommended. Electrolyte monitoring (potassium, sodium) recommended regularly. Haematological monitoring (WBC count) recommended. Surgery: Discontinue treatment where possible one day before surgery. Amlodipine: Safety and efficacy in hypertensive crisis not established. Cardiac failure — patients with heart failure should be treated with caution. Hepatic impairment — initiate at lower end of dosing range.
drug_interactions: Ramipril — Contraindicated: Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with sacubitril/valsartan, extracorporeal treatments leading to contact of blood with negatively charged surfaces, combination with aliskiren in patients with diabetes or moderate to severe renal impairment. Not recommended: Potassium salts, potassium-retaining diuretics or other drugs that may increase kalaemia — close monitoring required. Caution: Antihypertensive agents and other substances with antihypertensive potential (e.g. nitrates, tricyclic antidepressants, anaesthetics) — potentiation of antihypertensive effect. Vasopressor sympathomimetics — may reduce antihypertensive effect. Allopurinol, immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, procainamide, cytostatics — increased likelihood of haematological reactions. Lithium salts — lithium excretion may be reduced. Antidiabetic agents — ACE inhibitors may reduce insulin resistance. Vildagliptin, mTOR inhibitors, NEP inhibitors — increased incidence of angioedema. NSAIDs — attenuation of antihypertensive effect, risk of worsening of renal function. Heparin — rise in serum potassium. Alcohol — Ramipril may potentiate the effect of alcohol. Amlodipine — CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase amlodipine exposure resulting in increased risk of hypotension. CYP3A4 inducers — blood pressure should be monitored and dose adjustment considered. Dantrolene (infusion) — risk of lethal ventricular fibrillation with hyperkalemia — avoid co-administration. Tacrolimus — risk of increased tacrolimus blood levels. Cyclosporine — variable increases of 0-40% in cyclosporine trough concentrations. Simvastatin — limit dose of simvastatin to 20 mg daily in patients on amlodipine.
drug_food_interactions: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice: Not specifically stated for Cardace® am. Absorption of ramipril is not significantly affected by food. Amlodipine bioavailability not affected by food.
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: Cardace® am must not be taken during pregnancy. Pregnancy must be excluded before starting treatment. If the patient becomes pregnant during treatment medication with Cardace® am must be replaced as soon as possible by a treatment regimen without ACE inhibitors. When ACE inhibitors have been administered to women in the second and third trimester there have been reports of harmful effects on the fetus and newborn child. Amlodipine: Safety in human pregnancy has not been established. Lactation: Cardace® am is not recommended during lactation. Alternative treatment with better established safety profiles are preferable. Amlodipine is excreted in human milk — proportion of the maternal dose received by the infant estimated at interquartile range of 3-7% with maximum of 15%.
monitoring_parameters: Monitor blood pressure. Monitor renal function particularly in initial weeks of treatment. Monitor serum potassium and serum sodium. Monitor WBC count to permit detection of possible leucopenia. Tacrolimus blood levels when amlodipine is co-administered. Cyclosporine levels when amlodipine is co-administered.
overdose_management: Overdose with ramipril: Excessive peripheral vasodilatation (marked hypotension, shock), bradycardia, electrolyte disturbances, renal failure. Management: Primary detoxification (gastric lavage, activated charcoal), alpha-1-adrenergic agonists, angiotensin II if available, volume and salt substitution. Overdose with amlodipine: Excessive peripheral vasodilatation and possibly reflex tachycardia. Marked and probably prolonged systemic hypotension up to and including shock with fatal outcome have been reported. Management: Active cardiovascular support, frequent monitoring of cardiac and respiratory function, elevation of extremities. A vasoconstrictor may be helpful in restoring vascular tone. Intravenous calcium gluconate may be beneficial in reversing the effects of calcium channel blockade. Charcoal up to 2 hours after administration of amlodipine may reduce absorption rate. Dialysis not likely to be of benefit.

symptoms: Elevated blood pressure (essential hypertension), headache, dizziness, cough, fatigue, bradycardia, oedema
indications: For the treatment of essential hypertension in adults.
mechanism_of_action: Ramipril: Ramiprilat, the active metabolite of the prodrug ramipril, inhibits the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, kininase II). Reduced angiotensin II formation and inhibition of bradykinin breakdown lead to vasodilation. Metoprolol Succinate: A selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor blocker. At therapeutic doses it reduces resting heart rate, increases exercise tolerance and reduces blood pressure by reducing cardiac output. Metoprolol is a CYP2D6 substrate — enzyme inhibitors may affect its plasma concentrations.
composition: Cardace® Meto 2.5: Each uncoated bilayer tablet contains Ramipril I.P. 2.5 mg + Metoprolol Succinate IP 23.75 mg (equivalent to Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg) (as extended release). Colour: Yellow Ferric Oxide. Cardace® Meto 5: Each uncoated bilayer tablet contains Ramipril I.P. 5 mg + Metoprolol Succinate IP 47.5 mg (equivalent to Metoprolol tartrate 50 mg) (as extended release). Colour: Red Ferric Oxide.
strength: Ramipril 2.5 mg or 5 mg + Metoprolol Succinate ER (equivalent to Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg or 50 mg)
adult_dosage: One tablet daily. The usual initial dosage is one tablet of Cardace Meto 2.5 (25mg/2.5mg) daily. If blood pressure remains uncontrolled after about 2-3 weeks of therapy the dose may be increased to metoprolol succinate ER and ramipril (50mg/5mg) daily. Further increases may be done until the desired therapeutic response is achieved or a usual maximum adult dosage of 10 mg of ramipril and 100 mg of metoprolol succinate ER daily is attained. Tablets have to be swallowed with sufficient amounts of liquid. The tablets must not be chewed or crushed and can be taken before, during or after a meal. The dosage should be individualized — as therapeutic response and adverse effects are related to plasma concentration poor metabolisers may require lower than normal doses.
pediatric_dosage: Safety and efficacy in pediatric population has not been established.
renal_dose_adjustment: The lowest effective dose is recommended for patients with renal impairment. Since the initial dose of ramipril in these patients is 1.25 mg this fixed dose combination is not suitable for initial therapy. The combination may be used later when the patient requires at least 2.5 mg of ramipril. In such patients maximum total daily dose of ramipril should not exceed 5 mg.
hepatic_dose_adjustment: The lowest effective dose is recommended for patients with hepatic dysfunction. Since the initial dose of ramipril in these patients is 1.25 mg this fixed dose combination is not suitable for initial therapy. The maximum total daily dose of ramipril should not exceed 5 mg. Dosage may need to be adjusted in patients with severe liver function disorder for metoprolol.
side_effects: Ramipril adverse reactions — Common: headache, dizziness, non-productive tickling cough, bronchitis, sinusitis, dyspnea, gastrointestinal inflammation, digestive disturbances, abdominal discomfort, dyspepsia, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash in particular maculo-papular, muscle spasms, myalgia, increase in blood potassium levels, hypotension, decrease in orthostatic blood pressure, syncope, chest pain, fatigue. Uncommon: eosinophilia, depressed mood, anxiety, confusional state, tachycardia, arrhythmia, palpitations, oedema peripheral, flushing, bronchospasm, nasal congestion, angioedema, alopecia, pruritus, renal impairment, blood urea increased, blood creatinine increased. Rare: white blood cell count decreased, haemolytic anaemia, severe anaphylactic reactions, SJS, TEN, erythema multiforme, pemphigus. Metoprolol adverse reactions: CNS, cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, hematologic, musculoskeletal, reproductive adverse reactions. Hypersensitive reactions, photosensitivity, taste disturbance, blurred vision, dry eyes, and tinnitus have been reported.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ramipril, metoprolol, to any beta blocker, to any other ACE inhibitor, or any of the excipients, history of angioedema, not to be used concomitantly with sacubitril/valsartan therapy (do not initiate Cardace® Meto until sacubitril/valsartan is eliminated from the body), haemodynamically relevant renal artery stenosis bilateral or unilateral, hypotensive or haemodynamically unstable states, with aliskiren-containing medicines in patients with diabetes or moderate to severe renal impairment, with AIIRAs in patients with diabetic nephropathy, during pregnancy, second or third degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, unstable decompensated heart failure, clinically significant sinus bradycardia (<50/min), sick sinus syndrome, severe disorder of peripheral perfusion, hypotension (systolic BP below 100 mmHg), sinoatrial block, bronchial asthma and severe COPD, untreated pheochromocytoma, metabolic acidosis, patients with suspected acute MI if pulse rate is lower than 50 bpm or PQ interval longer than 0.24 s or systolic BP lower than 100 mmHg. Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors and extracorporeal treatments leading to contact of blood with negatively charged surfaces must be avoided. Concomitant intravenous administration of calcium channel blockers of verapamil or diltiazem type is contraindicated.
warnings_precautions: Ramipril — Angioedema: Angioedema occurring during treatment necessitates immediate discontinuation. Emergency treatment includes immediate administration of epinephrine. An increased risk of angioedema is possible with concomitant use of other drugs which may cause angioedema. Dual blockade of RAAS: Not recommended. Patients with hyper-stimulated renin angiotensin system are at risk of an acute pronounced fall in blood pressure and deterioration of renal function. Metoprolol — In chronic obstructive disease metoprolol may cause increased resistance in the respiratory tract. Patients with bronchospastic diseases should not use beta blockers. Diabetes: Metoprolol may mask some of the symptoms of hypoglycemia. Heart failure: Beta-adrenergic block may reduce myocardial contractility and exacerbate heart failure. AV conduction disorder: If bradycardia develops reduce dose or discontinue entirely. Therapy should not be discontinued suddenly but gradually over 10-14 days. Pheochromocytoma: Metoprolol may be used only after starting treatment with an alpha blocker. Thyrotoxicosis: Metoprolol may mask symptoms — administer with caution. Before surgery: Inform anaesthetist. Anaphylactic shock has a more severe course in patients treated with beta blockers. Monitoring of renal function, electrolytes and WBC count recommended for ramipril.
drug_interactions: Ramipril — Contraindicated: ACE inhibitors with sacubitril/valsartan, extracorporeal treatments with negatively charged surfaces, combination with aliskiren in patients with diabetes or moderate to severe renal impairment, AIIRAs in patients with diabetic nephropathy. Not recommended: Potassium salts, potassium-retaining diuretics — close monitoring required. Caution: Antihypertensive agents and other substances with antihypertensive potential — potentiation of antihypertensive effect. Vasopressor sympathomimetics. Lithium salts — toxicity risk. Antidiabetic agents — ACE inhibitors may reduce insulin resistance. Vildagliptin, mTOR inhibitors, NEP inhibitors — increased incidence of angioedema. NSAIDs — attenuation of antihypertensive effect. Heparin — rise in serum potassium. Alcohol — ramipril may potentiate the effect of alcohol. Metoprolol — Monoamine oxidase inhibitors: Not recommended. Ergotamine: Caution due to peripheral circulation effects. Clonidine: Beta blockers may accentuate rebound hypertension after clonidine discontinuation. Alpha blockers: Elevated risk of orthostatic hypotension. Calcium channel blockers (verapamil and diltiazem type): Risk of hypotension, AV conduction disorders, left ventricular insufficiency. Antiarrhythmics (Class I) and amiodarone: May increase negative inotropic and dromotropic effect. Cardiac glycosides: Deepening of negative chronotropic effect. Nitrates: May increase hypotension. CYP2D6 inhibitors (antiarrhythmics, antiretrovirals, antihistamines, fungicides, cimetidine, antimalarials, antidepressants such as bupropion, paroxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline): May elevate metoprolol plasma concentration. Lidocaine: Metoprolol may reduce clearance. Diltiazem: Sinus arrest may occur. Amiodarone, digoxin, diltiazem, verapamil, flecainide, ivabradine — risk of sinus arrest when combined with metoprolol.
pregnancy_lactation: Pregnancy: Cardace® Meto must not be taken during pregnancy. If the patient becomes pregnant medication with Cardace® Meto must be replaced as soon as possible by a treatment regimen without ACE inhibitors. Lactation: Cardace® Meto is not recommended during lactation.
monitoring_parameters: Monitor blood pressure. Monitor renal function particularly in initial weeks of treatment. Monitor serum potassium and serum sodium. Monitor WBC count. Carefully monitor patients with ischaemic heart disease during gradual withdrawal of metoprolol.

symptoms: Tachyarrhythmias, rapid heart rate, palpitations, symptoms of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation
indications: Tachyarrhythmias associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome. Atrial flutter and fibrillation when other drugs cannot be used. All types of tachyarrhythmias of paroxysmal nature including: supraventricular, nodal and ventricular tachycardias, ventricular fibrillation, when other drugs cannot be used. Treatment should be initiated and normally monitored only under hospital or specialist supervision. Oral amiodarone is indicated only for the treatment of severe rhythm disorders not responding to other therapies or when other treatments cannot be used.
mechanism_of_action: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic agent that prolongs the action potential duration and the refractory period in all cardiac tissues. It inhibits alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors, slows sinus heart rate, slows AV conduction and prolongs the QT interval (QT prolongation is related to prolonged repolarisation). Amiodarone exhibits a low torsadogenic activity despite QT interval prolongation. Amiodarone and/or its metabolite desethylamiodarone inhibit CYP1A1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and P-glycoprotein. Amiodarone contains iodine and thus may interfere with radio-iodine uptake. Amiodarone is strongly protein bound and has an average plasma half-life of 50 days (reported range 20-100 days).
composition: Cordarone®: Each uncoated tablet contains Amiodarone Hydrochloride I.P. 100 mg. Cordarone® X: Each uncoated tablet contains Amiodarone Hydrochloride I.P. 200 mg.
adult_dosage: In all cases the patient's management must be judged on the individual response and well-being. Initial stabilization: Treatment should be started with 200 mg three times a day and may be continued for 1 week. The dosage should then be reduced to 200 mg twice daily for a further week. Maintenance: After the initial period the dosage should be reduced to 200 mg daily or less if appropriate. Rarely the patient may require a higher maintenance dose. The 100 mg tablet should be used to titrate the minimum dosage required to maintain control of the arrhythmia. The maintenance dose should be regularly reviewed especially where this exceeds 200 mg daily. Elderly: Use minimum effective dose, may be more susceptible to bradycardia and conduction defects. Amiodarone is for oral administration.

missed_dose_instructions: Very common (≥10%): Corneal microdeposits, benign gastrointestinal disorders (nausea, vomiting, dysgeusia), isolated increase in serum transaminases, photosensitivity. Common (≥1% and <10%): Bradycardia (generally moderate and dose-related), hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism (sometimes fatal), acute liver disorders with high serum transaminases and/or jaundice including hepatic failure (sometimes fatal), extrapyramidal tremor, nightmares, sleep disorders, pulmonary toxicity (alveolar/interstitial pneumonitis or fibrosis, pleuritis, BOOP), sometimes fatal, slate grey or bluish pigmentations of the skin with prolonged treatment and high daily dosages. Uncommon: Onset or worsening of arrhythmia (sometimes followed by cardiac arrest), conduction disturbances (sinoatrial block, AV block of various degrees), peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy and/or myopathy. Very rare: Marked bradycardia or sinus arrest, optic neuropathy/neuritis (may progress to blindness), haemolytic anaemia, aplastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, chronic liver disease (pseudo alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis) sometimes fatal, cerebellar ataxia, benign intracranial hypertension, headache, SIADH, vasculitis, epididymitis, impotence, erythema during radiotherapy, skin rashes, exfoliative dermatitis, alopecia. Not known: Neutropenia, agranulocytosis, torsade de pointes, primary graft dysfunction post cardiac transplant, pancreatitis/acute pancreatitis, dry mouth, constipation, granuloma including bone marrow granuloma, angioneurotic oedema, anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reaction including shock, decreased appetite, lupus like syndrome, confusional state/delirium, hallucination, parkinsonism, parosmia, libido decreased, pulmonary haemorrhage, urticaria, eczema, severe skin reactions sometimes fatal including toxic epidermal necrolysis/Stevens-Johnson syndrome, bullous dermatitis, DRESS.
